title: Reaction wheel failures leave Swift rescue mission spinning in orbit
gist: Katalyst Space Technologies' Link satellite, built in nine months under a $30 million NASA contract to boost the 22-year-old Swift gamma-ray observatory out of a decaying orbit, has lost two of three reaction wheels and some cold gas thruster function, leaving it spinning with sporadic comms. Katalyst is repurposing the xenon electric thrusters for attitude control, and NASA's astrophysics director had already framed the attempt itself as a success regardless of outcome.

insights.claim: Two of the three reaction wheels on Katalyst Space Technologies' Link satellite are not operable and there is partial loss of function in its cold gas thruster system, causing the spacecraft to spin with sporadic communications.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Attitude control loss is typically mission-ending for rendezvous operations; this is a live test of the servicing thesis.
insights.quote: Preliminary investigation shows that two of Link’s three reaction wheels currently are not operable, and there is some loss of functionality in its cold gas thruster system
insights.locator: The Link satellite developed by Katalyst Space Technologies

insights.claim: Katalyst is now calling on Link's xenon-fueled electric thrusters to stabilize attitude, a task they were never designed to perform.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Off-design use of the propulsion reserved for orbit raising consumes the margin needed for the actual Swift boost.
insights.locator: Katalyst is now calling upon the electric thrusters

insights.claim: Link is still generating sufficient electrical power and remains in contact with ground teams, which gives engineers time to develop a fix for the reaction wheel problem.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Power and comms holding means the mission is impaired, not lost; watch for a revised approach plan rather than abandonment.
insights.locator: Katalyst’s Link spacecraft is still generating sufficient electrical power

insights.claim: Katalyst plans to update Link's guidance, navigation and control software for the degraded configuration, then re-evaluate the approach and capture of Swift depending on approach safety and spacecraft health.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Software-defined recovery of a hardware failure is the key capability claim for the commercial servicing sector.
insights.locator: After reestablishing stable attitude and further investigating spacecraft status

insights.claim: Without a rescue, NASA's Swift observatory will reenter the atmosphere and burn up within the next few months, since the nearly 22-year-old spacecraft has no propulsion system of its own.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: A hard, near-term deadline means there is no time for a second attempt if Link fails.
insights.locator: Without a rescue, Swift is on track to reenter the atmosphere

insights.claim: NASA wants Swift preserved because it is one of the only missions in the agency's fleet tuned to detect gamma-ray bursts, the most powerful explosions in the known Universe.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Irreplaceable instrument capability is what justifies paying for on-orbit servicing rather than replacement.
insights.locator: NASA officials want to keep Swift going

insights.claim: NASA is paying Katalyst $30 million for the rescue service, a price point that sets the reference for commercial satellite life-extension contracts.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: A $30 million benchmark for extending a flagship science asset is the unit economics number for the servicing market.
insights.quote: NASA is paying Katalyst $30 million for the rescue service.

insights.claim: Link must raise its orbit with xenon electric thrusters to rendezvous with Swift about 200 miles above Earth, then attach with three robotic arms before firing again to boost Swift's orbit.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: The mission profile shows the full technical stack a servicing provider must demonstrate: raise, rendezvous, capture, boost.
insights.locator: The electric thrusters are one of the most critical elements

themes.theme: Commercial servicing as a NASA experiment

insights.claim: NASA gave Katalyst just nine months to build and launch the Link satellite, an unusually fast timeline for a mission this complex, and Katalyst delivered for rocket integration in early June.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Nine-month build-to-launch is the schedule benchmark commercial servicing startups will now be measured against.
insights.locator: With Swift’s orbit rapidly decaying, NASA gave Katalyst nine months

insights.claim: The mission launched July 3 aboard an air-launched Northrop Grumman Pegasus XL rocket after poor weather and a technical glitch with the rocket pushed the date.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Pegasus XL remains the niche option for time-critical small launches, but adds schedule risk to already tight missions.
insights.locator: The Link mission began July 3 with a ride to orbit

insights.claim: NASA is explicitly using the Swift rescue as a technology demonstration to test the mettle of the commercial satellite servicing industry, not just to extend one telescope's life.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Outcome will shape whether NASA funds a broader servicing procurement line; a public failure slows the whole category.
insights.locator: Extending Swift’s scientific mission was not the only consideration

insights.claim: NASA astrophysics division director Shawn Domagal-Goldman said before the anomaly that he already considered the mission a success simply because the attempt was being made, pre-setting a low bar for judging the outcome.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Expectation management from the customer means a technical failure may not dent NASA's appetite for servicing contracts.
insights.quote: From a programmatics standpoint, I consider this a success already, just from the fact that we’re even going to try this
insights.locator: No matter the outcome of the Swift rescue attempt

insights.claim: Link principal investigator Kieran Wilson said before launch that power and communications are the fundamental systems that matter, because a spacecraft that functions at that level gives the team flexibility to work through rendezvous problems.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Gives the diagnostic hierarchy for judging whether a struggling servicing mission is recoverable.
insights.quote: Those are a lot of the basic things that most of the engineering team gets very concerned about
